body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Loss of more than 25% of blood volume can cause shock.
Think of internal as well as external bleeding.
Check inside bulky clothing and under the patient.
Steps: direct pressure, then packing, then tourniquet.
Tourniquet: last resort for massive limb bleeding.
Band 7.5 to 10 cm, wide and flat, never wire or rope.
Place as close above the wound as possible.
Note the time of application.
Over 1 hour from care: loosen slowly at 60 min while pressing.
Commercial tourniquets: CAT, SOFT.
Pelvic sling centred on the greater trochanters.

deeper.title: Why width matters for a tourniquet
deeper.html:
A narrow cord concentrates force on a thin strip of skin: it cuts and crushes nerves and muscle before it squeezes the artery shut. A band 7.5 to 10 cm wide spreads the same pressure over a larger area, closing the artery at lower pressure with less tissue damage.

Source: the lecture's tourniquet application slide.

deeper.title: Why a sling helps a broken pelvis
deeper.html:
An open-book pelvic fracture enlarges the pelvic volume, and torn pelvic veins can lose litres of blood into that space. Binding the pelvis at the level of the greater trochanters closes the ring, reduces the volume the blood can fill and brings the bone ends together, which helps the bleeding stop.

Source: the lecture's pelvic sling slides.

figure.caption: Escalating steps to stop external bleeding. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Assess: site, artery or vein, >25% loss?

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Commonest mechanism: VF or pulseless VT.
Unresponsive + abnormal (agonal) breathing = cardiac arrest.
Pulse check by professionals: 10 seconds at most.
In doubt, start CPR.
Compressions: lower half of sternum, 5 to 6 cm, 100 to 120/min, full recoil.
Ratio 30:2 if trained; otherwise continuous compressions.
AED pads: right infraclavicular, left mid-axillary; must not touch.
Shockable: VF and pulseless VT. Non-shockable: asystole and PEA.
CPR for 2 minutes between rhythm checks.
SCD is about 50% of cardiovascular deaths.

deeper.title: Why full recoil matters
deeper.html:
Compressions push blood out of the heart, but the heart can only refill while the chest springs back. Leaning on the chest between compressions keeps intrathoracic pressure high, blocks venous return, and the next compression has little to push. That is why the lecture insists on full recoil and no leaning.

Source: the lecture's high-quality chest compression slide.

deeper.title: Why early defibrillation matters so much
deeper.html:
Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic electrical activity that pumps nothing; a shock resets all cells at once so the sinus node can take over. The chance that a shock works falls quickly with every minute without CPR, as the heart muscle runs out of energy. CPR buys time, but the AED is what actually restarts a fibrillating heart.

Source: the lecture's AED and rhythm slides.

figure.caption: Recognise, alert, compress, ventilate, defibrillate. Schematic drawn for this site.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Shock: circulatory failure to oxygenate tissues.
Four types: cardiogenic, hypovolaemic, distributive, obstructive.
MAP = CO × SVR; CO = SV × HR.
SV depends on preload, contractility, afterload.
CaO2 = 1.34 × Hb × SaO2; TaO2 = CaO2 × CO.
Fick: VO2 = CO × (CaO2 - CvO2).
Hypoperfusion → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acidosis.
Capillary refill > 3 s is a sign of hypoperfusion.
Obstructive: tamponade, PE, tension pneumothorax.
Treatment: oxygen, fluids, catecholamines, plus the cause.

deeper.title: Why blood pressure can look normal in early shock
deeper.html:
The baroreflex raises heart rate and constricts vessels as soon as flow falls, so MAP = CO × SVR can stay normal while cardiac output is already low. Tachycardia, cold mottled skin and rising lactate appear first. Waiting for hypotension means recognising shock late.

Source: the lecture's baroreflex and compensatory changes slides.

deeper.title: Why haemorrhage hits oxygen delivery twice
deeper.html:
Oxygen delivery is cardiac output times arterial oxygen content. Bleeding lowers output (less preload) and lowers haemoglobin, so both terms fall at once. That is why the lecture notes that in haemorrhagic shock anaemia adds to the drop in oxygen transport.

Source: the lecture's hypovolaemic shock slide.

figure.caption: MAP = CO × SVR and the four families of shock. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: MAP = CO × SVR CO = SV × HR
Signs: mottling, CRT > 3 s, confusion, oliguria, lactate

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: GI jobs: motility, secretion, digestion, absorption, storage, endocrine, protection, expulsion.
Liver gets 25% of CO; portal vein 75% of flow, 50% of O2.
Ammonia → urea in the liver.
True liver function tests: PT and albumin.
Lipase: rises 4-8 h, lasts 8-14 days, more specific than amylase.
Amylase: rises 2-12 h, normal by 3-5 days, non-specific.
Paracetamol is the commonest cause of drug-induced liver injury; antidote NAC.
Mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion; CT angiography first.
Watershed zones: Griffiths' and Sudeck's points.
Pancreatitis: 80% gallstones or alcohol; ERCP for biliary obstruction.

deeper.title: Why PT and albumin, not enzymes, measure liver function
deeper.html:
Transaminases leak from damaged hepatocytes, so they measure injury, not how much liver still works; they can even fall as the liver dies. The liver alone makes albumin and most clotting factors, so a prolonged prothrombin time or low albumin shows that synthetic capacity is failing. The short half-life of clotting factors makes PT the faster warning.

Source: the lecture's liver function slides.

deeper.title: Why mesenteric ischaemia hurts before the belly is tender
deeper.html:
Early on, the ischaemia is in the bowel mucosa and wall, which sends deep visceral pain but does not irritate the parietal peritoneum. Tenderness and rigidity only appear once the whole wall is necrotic and inflames the peritoneum. By then the bowel may be dead, which is why pain out of proportion to the examination must trigger CT angiography early.

Source: the lecture's mesenteric ischaemia pathophysiology slide.

figure.caption: Liver function tests and three life-threatening GI emergencies. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Liver: 25% of CO; portal vein 75% of flow
True liver function: PT and albumin
Mesenteric ischaemia: pain > signs, CT angio

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Adrenal cortex: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens).
Addison disease appears at about 90% loss of adrenal function.
Adrenal crisis: refractory hypotension, may mimic septic shock.
Adrenal crisis labs: low Na, high K, low glucose.
Suspect it if prednisone > 7.5 mg/day for > 3 weeks.
Treat with saline and hydrocortisone after sending cortisol and ACTH.
Alpha → glucagon, beta → insulin, delta → somatostatin.
DKA: hyperglycaemia + ketones + acidosis; Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath.
DKA: serum K high but total body K depleted; avoid hypokalaemia.
Thyroid storm: HR > 140, fever > 41 °C, CNS dysfunction.
Storm treatment: beta-blocker, PTU/methimazole, dexamethasone, iodine, cooling.

deeper.title: Why adrenal crisis resists vasopressors
deeper.html:
Cortisol is permissive for catecholamines: it keeps vascular receptors responsive and supports their synthesis. Without cortisol, vessels respond poorly to noradrenaline and the heart may not even speed up. That is why the lecture says to think of adrenal crisis when hypotension persists despite fluids and several vasopressors.

Source: the lecture's adrenal crisis critical presentation slide.

deeper.title: Why insulin can make DKA potassium fall dangerously
deeper.html:
In DKA potassium is pushed out of cells by acidosis and lost in the urine, so the blood level looks high while the body is depleted. Insulin drives potassium back into cells within hours, unmasking the deficit and risking arrhythmias. Hence 'avoid hypokalaemia' in the treatment list.

Source: the lecture's DKA pathophysiology and treatment slides.

figure.caption: The three crises of the lecture and their first steps. Schematic drawn for this site.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Innate: first line, fast, non-specific; adaptive: specific, days, memory.
Innate reactions: inflammation and antiviral defence (NK cells, type I IFN).
PRRs detect PAMPs and DAMPs.
NK cells kill cells lacking MHC class I.
IgA deficiency is the commonest primary immunodeficiency.
SCID: no T or B cells; needs bone marrow transplant.
HIV destroys CD4+ T cells.
Type I hypersensitivity: IgE, mast cells, histamine, minutes.
Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline in the thigh without delay.
Rejection: hyperacute (antibodies), acute (T cells), chronic (fibrosis).
Calcineurin inhibitors: ciclosporin, tacrolimus.

deeper.title: Why adrenaline goes in the thigh muscle
deeper.html:
The vastus lateralis is large and well perfused, so adrenaline injected there is absorbed quickly and reliably, faster than under the skin. Adrenaline reverses the key problems of anaphylaxis at once: it constricts leaky vessels, opens the airways and supports the heart. Antihistamines and steroids are too slow to save a life on their own.

Source: the lecture's anaphylaxis treatment slide.

deeper.title: Why memory makes vaccines work
deeper.html:
A first exposure takes days to produce antibodies because rare specific lymphocytes must multiply. Vaccination leaves many memory B and T cells behind, so a real infection triggers a response that is faster and stronger, often clearing the microbe before disease develops. Boosters top up this memory when it fades.

Source: the lecture's vaccination and primary/secondary response slides.

figure.caption: Innate and adaptive arms, and what goes wrong. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Innate: barriers, phagocytes, complement, NK, IFN

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Normal ICP 5 to 15 mmHg; raised ICP ≥ 20 mmHg.
Monro-Kellie: brain + blood + CSF in a fixed box.
CPP = MAP - ICP.
Autoregulation keeps CBF constant for CPP 60 to 160 mmHg.
CPP < 60: ischaemia; > 160: hypertensive encephalopathy.
Brain = 2-3% of body mass, 20% of circulating blood.
Oedema: vasogenic, cytotoxic, interstitial, osmotic.
Steroids help vasogenic (tumour) oedema.
Burr hole for epidural haematoma with deterioration.
Hydrocephalus is treated with shunts.

deeper.title: Why a small extra volume can suddenly be fatal
deeper.html:
At first the skull compensates: CSF is pushed into the spinal canal and venous blood leaves the head, so ICP barely changes. Once these reserves are used up, the pressure-volume curve turns steep and a few extra millilitres cause a large jump in ICP. This is why a patient with a haematoma can talk, then deteriorate quickly.

Source: the lecture's pressure-volume relationship slide.

deeper.title: Why CO2 matters to the brain
deeper.html:
Carbon dioxide dilates cerebral vessels. A rise in PaCO2 increases cerebral blood volume and therefore ICP, while a fall constricts vessels and lowers it. That is why ventilation of a head-injured patient is carefully controlled, as the lecture's PaO2/PaCO2 blood-flow figure shows.

Source: the lecture's cerebral blood flow slide.

figure.caption: The Monro-Kellie doctrine and the vicious circle of raised ICP. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Rigid skull: any rise in volume raises ICP

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: First aid aims: preserve life, prevent worsening, promote recovery.
Secure the scene before acting; protect yourself with PPE.
Three Cs: Check, Call, Care.
Primary survey: ABCDE.
Emergency number in Morocco: 15.
Breathing check: look, listen, feel, maximum 10 seconds.
Suspect a cervical spine injury after falls and major trauma.
Airway: head tilt with chin lift, or jaw thrust.
Unconscious and breathing: recovery position (left side in pregnancy).
Complete choking: no speech, no cough, no air exchange.
Adult choking: back blows then Heimlich; infant: 5 back blows, 5 chest thrusts.
Obese or pregnant victim: chest thrusts, not abdominal.

deeper.title: Why the scene comes before the victim
deeper.html:
An injured rescuer turns one casualty into two and removes the only person able to help. That is why the lecture puts scene safety before any examination: switching off engines, spotting live wires or rising water, and wearing gloves all protect the rescue itself.

Source: the lecture's secure-the-scene slides.

deeper.title: Why the recovery position works
deeper.html:
Lying on the back, an unconscious person's tongue and soft palate sag onto the pharynx, and any vomit pools where it can be inhaled. Turning them on their side lets gravity pull the tongue forward and drain fluids out of the mouth, so the airway stays open without anyone holding it.

Source: the lecture's unresponsive-victim slides.

figure.caption: Protect, check, call, care: the order the lecture teaches. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Airway: head tilt, chin lift, jaw thrust

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Renal blood flow = 20% of cardiac output.
Glomerular capillaries lie between two arterioles.
Normal GFR ≈ 120-130 mL/min/1.73 m² (about 180 L/day).
GFR falls about 1 mL/min/year after 40.
Autoregulation for perfusion pressure 80-180 mmHg.
Low NaCl at the macula densa → renin release.
Prerenal AKI is commonest (40-55%) and reversible.
ATN is the commonest intrinsic cause.
Commonest postrenal cause: bladder outlet obstruction.
Diuretics only for fluid overload.
Dialysis: refractory overload, uraemic pericarditis, severe electrolyte/acid-base disorders.
Urine < 400 mL/day = worse prognosis.

deeper.title: Why prerenal AKI is reversible and ATN is not
deeper.html:
In prerenal AKI the tubules are healthy; they are just underperfused and avidly reabsorb sodium and water. Restore perfusion and GFR returns within hours. If hypoperfusion lasts, tubular cells die and slough into the lumen: that is ATN, and recovery then needs the epithelium to regrow over days to weeks.

Source: the lecture's prerenal AKI slides.

deeper.title: Why hyperkalaemia is the dangerous complication
deeper.html:
The kidney excretes most daily potassium. When GFR collapses, potassium from diet and damaged cells accumulates, and acidosis shifts more out of cells. High potassium destabilises cardiac membranes and can cause fatal arrhythmias, which is why severe electrolyte disorders are an indication for dialysis.

Source: the lecture's complications and dialysis slides.

figure.caption: Prerenal, intrinsic and postrenal causes. Schematic drawn for this site.

provenance.note: Trauma injuries and burns.pdf (First Aid and Vital Functions, Pr Amal Haoudar)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Trauma ABCDE: airway with C-spine, circulation with haemorrhage control, exposure without hypothermia.
Palpable pulse ≈ minimum SBP: radial 80, femoral 70, carotid 60 mmHg.
Five sites of major haemorrhage: chest, abdomen, retroperitoneum, thigh, external.
Never force a person into a position.
Splint the joint above and below; check neurovascular status before and after.
Remove motorcycle helmets pre-hospital with two rescuers.
Amputated part: moist wrap, sealed bag, ice water, never frozen.
Chemical burns: water at least 10 minutes, no neutraliser.
Cool burns with water about 30 minutes; beware hypothermia in large burns.
Remove jewellery from burned fingers and toes.

deeper.title: Why cooling helps only early
deeper.html:
Heat keeps damaging tissue for several minutes after the source is removed, as stored heat spreads deeper. Early cooling pulls that heat out and limits the depth of the burn. After about 30 minutes the damage is already set, so cooling can only ease pain, which is exactly the time limit the lecture gives.

Source: the lecture's burn cooling slide.

deeper.title: Why a full-face helmet has to come off
deeper.html:
A full-face helmet hides the airway and the face and makes ventilation impossible. Because of its bulk it also pushes a lying victim's head into flexion. Removing it carefully with two rescuers keeps the neck in line while giving access to the airway.

Source: the lecture's helmet removal slides.

figure.caption: Primary survey, then spinal protection, splinting and burn care. Schematic drawn for this site.
